items.readable_text:
Content:
The orthogonal projection of a vector [MATH: \mathbf{x}] onto a span [MATH: \textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}] is the vector in [MATH: \textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}] that is "closest" to [MATH: \mathbf{x}.] Let's work an example to clarify what we mean by "closest."

Content:
Consider the following two vectors:

Content:
[MATH: [5; − 1; 0; 1]]

Content:
Geometrically, [MATH: \mathbf{x}] can be written as the sum of a vector [MATH: k{\mathbf{a}}] that lies in [MATH: \textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}] and
another vector [MATH: \mathbf{z}] that belongs to the orthogonal complement of [MATH: \textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}], as illustrated in the picture below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/15f9e2cdbaf7812381f739a8602f4674]

Content:
The vector [MATH: k\mathbf a] is called the orthogonal projection of [MATH: \mathbf{x}] onto [MATH: \textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}.]

Content:
Symbolically, we can write the vector [MATH: \mathbf{x}] as the sum

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{x} = k \mathbf{a} + \mathbf{z},]

Content:
for some [MATH: k \in \mathbb{R}] and [MATH: {\mathbf{z}} \perp \mathbf{a}.]

Content:
To compute the orthogonal projection [MATH: k \mathbf{a},] we can first find the dot product of both sides of the equation above with [MATH: \mathbf{a}] to get

Content:
[MATH: x ⋅ a|= (ka + z) ⋅ a; x ⋅ a|= k(a ⋅ a) + z ⋅ a.]

Content:
Since [MATH: \mathbf{a} \perp \mathbf{z},] we have [MATH: \mathbf{z} \cdot \mathbf{a} = 0.] As a result,
[MATH: x ⋅ a|= k(a ⋅ a); k|= (x ⋅ a)/(a ⋅ a); k|= (5 ⋅ 3 + (− 1) ⋅ (− 6) + 0 ⋅ 0 + 1 ⋅ 6)/(3^{2} + (− 6)^{2} + 6^{2}); k|= (1)/(3).]

Content:
Therefore, the orthogonal projection is

Content:
[MATH: ka = (1)/(3)[3; − 6; 0; 6] = [1; − 2; 0; 2].]

Content:
Note: There is a shortcut! Instead of going through this process each time, we can compute the orthogonal projection of [MATH: \mathbf{x}] onto [MATH: \textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}] using the following formula:

Content:
[MATH: proj_{a}x|= (a ⋅ x)/(a ⋅ a)a]

The orthogonal projection of [MATH: \mathbf{a}] onto [MATH: \textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{b}\}] is given by

Given the vector [MATH: \mathbf{x}] and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of [MATH: \mathbf{x}] onto the solution space of the system.
[MATH: [− 10; 20; 2]]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we need to find the basis of the solution space of the system.

Consider the augmented matrix [MATH: M] of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

[MATH: M|= [1|1|4|0; 1|2|0|0]|R_{2}|:=R_{2} − R_{1}; ∼[1|1|4|0; 0|1|− 4|0].] In the reduced matrix above, there are [MATH: 2] pivot columns ([MATH: 1]st and [MATH: 2]nd). Thus, [MATH: x_3] is a free variable. Now, from the second equation, we get [MATH: x_2=4x_3.] Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

[MATH: x_1+4x_3+4x_3= 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x_1=-8x_3.]

So, the general solution is [MATH: [− 8x_{3}; 4x_{3}; x_{3}]] Consequently, [MATH: [− 8; 4; 1]] is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of [MATH: \mathbf{x}] onto the solution space of the system:

[MATH: proj_{b}x|= (x ⋅ b)/(b ⋅ b)b; = ((− 10) ⋅ (− 8) + 20 ⋅ 4 + 2 ⋅ 1)/((− 8)^{2} + 4^{2} + 1^{2})b; = (80 + 80 + 2)/(64 + 16 + 1)b; = (162)/(81)b; = 2b; = 2[− 8; 4; 1]; = [− 16; 8; 2]]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The orthogonal projection of a vector [MATH: \mathbf{x}] onto a span [MATH: \textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}] is the vector in [MATH: \textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}] that is "closest" to [MATH: \mathbf{x}.] Let's work an example to clarify what we mean by "closest."

Content:
Consider the following two vectors:

Content:
[MATH: [5; − 1; 0; 1]]

Content:
Geometrically, [MATH: \mathbf{x}] can be written as the sum of a vector [MATH: k{\mathbf{a}}] that lies in [MATH: \textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}] and
another vector [MATH: \mathbf{z}] that belongs to the orthogonal complement of [MATH: \textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}], as illustrated in the picture below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/15f9e2cdbaf7812381f739a8602f4674]

Content:
The vector [MATH: k\mathbf a] is called the orthogonal projection of [MATH: \mathbf{x}] onto [MATH: \textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}.]

Content:
Symbolically, we can write the vector [MATH: \mathbf{x}] as the sum

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{x} = k \mathbf{a} + \mathbf{z},]

Content:
for some [MATH: k \in \mathbb{R}] and [MATH: {\mathbf{z}} \perp \mathbf{a}.]

Content:
To compute the orthogonal projection [MATH: k \mathbf{a},] we can first find the dot product of both sides of the equation above with [MATH: \mathbf{a}] to get

Content:
[MATH: x ⋅ a|= (ka + z) ⋅ a; x ⋅ a|= k(a ⋅ a) + z ⋅ a.]

Content:
Since [MATH: \mathbf{a} \perp \mathbf{z},] we have [MATH: \mathbf{z} \cdot \mathbf{a} = 0.] As a result,
[MATH: x ⋅ a|= k(a ⋅ a); k|= (x ⋅ a)/(a ⋅ a); k|= (5 ⋅ 3 + (− 1) ⋅ (− 6) + 0 ⋅ 0 + 1 ⋅ 6)/(3^{2} + (− 6)^{2} + 6^{2}); k|= (1)/(3).]

Content:
Therefore, the orthogonal projection is

Content:
[MATH: ka = (1)/(3)[3; − 6; 0; 6] = [1; − 2; 0; 2].]

Content:
Note: There is a shortcut! Instead of going through this process each time, we can compute the orthogonal projection of [MATH: \mathbf{x}] onto [MATH: \textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}] using the following formula:

Content:
[MATH: proj_{a}x|= (a ⋅ x)/(a ⋅ a)a]

---

Item 2 — Example: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector onto a One-Dimensional Subspace

Example Prompt:
Let [MATH: [2; 9; − 1; − 1]] and [MATH: [2; 1; 0; 1]] Find the orthogonal projection of [MATH: \mathbf{a}] onto [MATH: \text{Span}\{\mathbf{b}\}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The orthogonal projection of [MATH: \mathbf{a}] onto [MATH: \textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{b}\}] is given by

[MATH: proj_{b}a|= (b ⋅ a)/(b ⋅ b)b; = (2 ⋅ 2 + 1 ⋅ 9 + 0 ⋅ (− 1) + 1 ⋅ (− 1))/(2^{2} + 1^{2} + 0^{2} + 1^{2})b; = (4 + 9 + 0 − 1)/(4 + 1 + 0 + 1)b; = (12)/(6)b; = 2b; = 2[2; 1; 0; 1]; = [4; 2; 0; 2].]

Item 5 — Tutorial: The Distance  Between a Vector and a One-Dimensional Subspace

Content:
We define the distance between the vector [MATH: \mathbf{x}] and the vector space [MATH: \textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}] to be
[MATH: \Vert \mathbf{x} - \text{proj}_{\mathbf{a}}\,\mathbf{x} \Vert.]

Content:
We can also define the angle [MATH: \theta] between the vector [MATH: \mathbf{x}] and the subspace [MATH: \textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}] to be the acute angle between the vector [MATH: \mathbf{x}] and its orthogonal projection [MATH: \text{proj}_{\mathbf{a}}\,\mathbf{x},] as shown in the diagram below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/b9a288e6c87399d2d3fa6d772b9e4895]

Content:
Finally, we now can represent the vector [MATH: \mathbf{x}] as a sum of two orthogonal vectors

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{x} = \underbrace{\textrm{proj}_{\mathbf{a}}\mathbf{x}}_{\large \mathbf{y}} + \underbrace{(\mathbf{x}-\textrm{proj}_{\mathbf{a}}\mathbf{x})}_{\large \mathbf{z}},]

Content:
where [MATH: \mathbf{y} \in \text{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}] and [MATH: \mathbf{z} \perp \text{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}.]

Content:
Note: The vector [MATH: \textbf{x}-\textrm{proj}_{\mathbf{a}}\mathbf{x},] whose norm [MATH: \| \textbf{x}-\textrm{proj}_{\mathbf{a}}\mathbf{x} \|] represents the distance from [MATH: \mathbf{x}] to [MATH: \mathbf{a},] is sometimes called the vector rejection of [MATH: \mathbf{x}] from [MATH: \mathbf{a}.]

---

Item 6 — Example: Calculating the Distance  Between a Vector and a One-Dimensional Subspace

Example Prompt:
Let [MATH: [4; − 4; 2; 2]] and [MATH: [1; − 1; 0; − 1]] If [MATH: \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{y} + \mathbf{z},] where [MATH: \mathbf{y} \in \text{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}] and [MATH: \mathbf{z} \perp \text{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\},] then find [MATH: \mathbf{z}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
A diagram of the situation is provided below:

[IMG: /graphics/1a8d9c2a40956965eaef1293fc216d15]

First, we find the orthogonal projection of [MATH: \mathbf{x}] onto [MATH: \textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: proj_{a}x|= (a ⋅ x)/(a ⋅ a)a; = (1 ⋅ 4 + (− 1) ⋅ (− 4) + 0 ⋅ 2 + (− 1) ⋅ 2)/(1^{2} + (− 1)^{2} + 0^{2} + (− 1)^{2})a; = (4 + 4 + 0 − 2)/(1 + 1 + 0 + 1)a; = (6)/(3)a; = 2a; = 2[1; − 1; 0; − 1]; = [2; − 2; 0; − 2]]

Therefore, we get the following:

[MATH: y|= proj_{a}x = [2; − 2; 0; − 2]; z|= x − proj_{a}x = [4; − 4; 2; 2] − [2; − 2; 0; − 2] = [2; − 2; 2; 4]]

Notice that [MATH: \mathbf{y} \in \text{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}] and [MATH: \mathbf{z} \perp \text{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\},] as shown in the picture above.
